abs: EVEN THOUGH ITS POPULARITY as a seminar and lecture topic has recently declined on conference agenda, the problem of communication among key administrators has neither been resolved nor diminished. Much attention in the past has been devoted to an analysis of communication problems between levels within an organization. Relatively little attention has been given to the patterns and problems of communication between administrators at the highest level of organizations. However, an experiment in administrative communication which proved successful illustrates one approach to this recurrent dilemma. Faced with an organization which was doubling its size every three years, the operation of a campus whose complexity and problems were increasing at an even greater pace, and a limited number of skilled academic administrators, the college needed an immediate answer. A new type of stand-up meeting was an innovation that greatly improved top-level communication patterns.

abs: C ATCH PHRASES CAPTURE some of the flavor of administration. Among others, these include open systems, temporary, changing, dialectical, and problem-solving organizations, and existential executives. The approaches place at least as much emphasis upon interactions between organizations and their external environments as upon the internal workings of complex organizations, because the single organization, whatever its comprehensiveness, can accomplish little by itself. Because the interactions include individuals and organizations without formal to order each other around, concepts of hierarchy and executive responsibility provide insufficient operational guidance. There is a need, now in the early stages of articulation, to reorient public policy processes in these directions; to establish, for example, a variety of mechanisms that link national and local governments, academia, and the business community, among other circles of influence.1 Whatever the extent of demands from individual citizens and groups that they be able to participate, the demands seem linked more to policy than to electoral processes.2 The trends may portend, perhaps for the first time, a true synthesis of politics and administration, and the conceptualization and implementation of new processes may be the most important items on the agenda. This is because policy processes can determine who participates and, if properly designed, can decrease the likelihood of poor decisions and make it easier to reverse such decisions when they are made. For the most part, however, these new approaches have not been put to work in the most important policy processes. Recommendations for change in presidential processes, for example, tend to follow traditional models. One sees demands that the Department of State take charge of foreign policy, or that a Super Secretary standing above the Cabiet handle both foreign and military affairswith the assistance of a White House staff.3 Predictions of domestic superdepartments modeled after the Department of Defense have been followed by presidential requests to construct such departments in the hope they will encompass all the needed authority and resources. 5 This persistent drive for overhead consolidation may be marching us to the rear. The notion seems to remain that if an organization can only be made big enough, all we need do is erect walls around it, treat it as a closed system, and apply hallowed concepts of command and control. Traditional models do indeed have a strong grip; even the language of administration is inherently hierarchical, making it difficult to conceptualize alternatives or describe them when they exist. This article concentrates upon the past, present, and future implications of one such alternative. t: USAC: An Evolving Intergovernmental Mechanism for Urban Information Systems Development
abs: VIEWED BROADLY, the Urban Information Systems Inter-Agency Committee (USAC) is a dynamic mechanism for channeling federal resources to improve local government administration. Its specific purpose is to facilitate intergovernmental cooperation in urban information systems research and development. USAC is important because it is simultaneously conducting an experiment in product research and development and in administrative organization. The anticipated products are operationally based and integrated information systems. The administrative organization is an evolving network of relationships among many governmental and private units designed to build the prototype systems.

abs: THE HIGHER CIVIL SERVICE rest upon a persuasive rationale. Today the vast array of government responsibilities requires an unprecedented level of managerial competence. The diversity of modern government demands managers who able to move across organizational and functional lines, as well as a variety of professional specialists. This need for increased responsiveness, flexibility, and specialization requires singling out the top rungs of employees for special treatment. This familiar argument is bulwarked with envious comparisons. Separate systems for executive personnel, a brochure of the California State Personnel Board states, are the hallmark of many other [i.e., non-American] career public services, and private industry typically applies very different personnel practices to managerial personnel. 1 Given the rationale and the precedents, an examination of public service movements toward a separate career executive system is warranted. Two jurisdictions in the vanguard of this movement the national government and the California state government. The latter has had experience with a separate career executive system since 1963, and at the moment Congress has before it a proposal for instituting such a system.

abs: LET US BEGIN BY ASKING WHAT are the distinguishing qualities of a good regulatory agency. Granted that any public agency must begin with an honorable devotion to the public interest, we might list the main, specific qualities of a good regulatory agency as competence, independence, power, and vitality. These four qualities are not exhaustive; they overlap, interact, and reinforce each other; they may not even make up the best list of their kind, and it is certainly a current and not a permanent list. But these four qualities do have one very useful thing in common. They are qualities of the agency itself and not of the agency's work. They are qualities of the agency and are matters which the public and its government can do something about. To what extent a regulatory agency will be competent, independent, strong, and vital will, obviously, depend on many things. Our question is whether it will depend on the level of government of which the agency is part. There the record is mixed. Let's look at it.

abs: posed by its soaring budget (trebled in less than 15 years), its ponderous administrative machinery, its mounting list of social ills demanding solutions. It has elected to meet its challenges by a massive-and risky-restructuring of its 50,000-man Executive Department and a reshaping of the decision and control processes that it employs to manage its nearly $2 billion budget. That the commitment to change is of massive size is understandable, because the problems are likewise. That it is risky is less well understood, because what may be truly at risk in Massachusetts is the viability of management and stewardship of huge government enterprise. As this article will show, Massachusetts at the moment has everything going for it in tackling this task-more, perhaps, than any state in recent memory. What it does with its opportunity may well foretell the role that this newly pressured middle tier of government-the states-will play as this century winds toward a close.

Governance of the Municipality: Fracture and Divorce
abs: Four-fifths of our ten largest cities are losing population at the same time peripheral communities continue to boom. These suburbs have had no taste for consolidation with the central city, nor do they wish to unite with one another. So we have a fracture of some 81,000 local units of government competing for citizen support of their function and of their need for financing. What about the divorce? It is between the schools and nonschool local functions. Many authors separate government and schools as differing enterprises; yet as much as half of local public expenditures are for schools, and keen citizen interest is shown in the quality of the education provided. The divorce is tragic-especially as it fractures citizen interest and sharpens competition for the tax dollar. Jerome Zukosky, in directing a New York State study for the Twentieth Century Fund, states that in research and public hearings conducted to date, there has been no point in which general governments and school governments could be separated out in their impact on the decisions that shape the urban area. He laments, therefore, any study that separates concern with cities, towns, villages, and counties, and those of our public schools. Regional planning groups generally concern themselves with water and air resources, transportation and sanitation needs, and not with junior and senior high schools, for example, and their curriculum and noncurriculum impact. In the metropolitan area surrounding Arlington there have been some encouraging signs, first toward bringing a community college system to Northern Virginia. More recently, our Council of Governments is looking to the curriculum needs for more effective learning approaches to drug abuse problems.

abs: American mayor and the city manager found in the literature of public administration and political science are related to the realities of those offices in much the same way as Smokey the Bear is related to the grizzly bear of the Northwest. The literary figures are benign, simplified caricatures of complex and not completely tameable realities. It is true that in recent years some recognition of the potential power of these offices has begun to filter into the literature. The manager was recognized as a community leader by his own code of ethics.1 The code, however, makes no positive suggestion on how the manager is to express that leadership role. Officially, the mayor is still limited to presiding over council meetings and ceremonially representing the city.2 The realities of the mayors' leadership roles are beginning to be investigated.3 This article sketches some of the authors' preliminary findings on the interrelationships of mayors and managers in 45 council-manager cities with populations greater than 100,000, and some of the conceptions of managers and mayors suggested by an interpretation of the information collected. t: The Public Service in the Temporary Society
abs: But there is a question prior to these which requires attention. It concerns the changing nature and probable future directions of the society from which the public services are drawn, within which they operate, and which they are presumed to serve. This essay therefore begins with some observations about the society and its demands upon government, including some of the underlying dilemmas which seem to me most salient to the public service of the near future. Its second part is a discussion of the probable implications of these social directions and dilemmas for public administrative organizations, the public service, public personnel systems, and the universities.

abs: OFFICIALS, our nation has developed an enormous enthusiasm for the use of scientific technologies in the solution to public problems. We implicitly turn to the fix as a solution to many social and economic problems. Recently this enthusiasm has been focused upon our urban scene in a seeming desperate hope that technology can somehow help us break out of the apparent pathway to social disaster we amble along. With less hope, I suspect the converts to ecology also implicitly hold largely technological solutions to the fouling of our world; somehow science must find a way to re-establish our resource balance while at the same time maintaining our level of creature comforts.
